Active particle systems are composed of interacting, self-propelled particles that can model complex biological and physical systems.
The paper reviews two distinct types of animal behavior: animal contests (fights over resources) and cohesive swarms (midge swarms).
Nonreciprocal interactions violate Newton's third law and do not obey usual conservation laws of Newtonian mechanics.
The contestant interaction potential has two distinct local extrema: a minimum and a maximum, determined by the Lambert W function.
The model uses a Langevin equation to govern the spatio-temporal dynamics of contestant particles: ṙ_i = -η∇V_tot→i(r_i,{r_j}) + √(2D)ξ_i + activity.
The mobility parameter η has dimensions of L·F⁻¹T⁻¹ and sets the contribution of deterministic forces to contestant motion.
The diffusivity parameter D has dimensions of L²T⁻¹ and sets the contribution of stochastic forces to contestant motion.
The resource potential is typically modeled as V_res→i(r) = -p_i ln(|r| + ε), a logarithmic sink with parameters p and ε.
The contestant interaction potential combines logarithmic repulsion and an attractive Gaussian well.
The 'attention switch' mechanism uses a Heaviside step function to transition between resource-driven and rival-driven motion.
In the spider contest system, the resource potential is non-isotropic because males approach the female from the back and avoid its front.
The model can describe both single-stage and two-stage contest escalation schemes.
Adaptivity is a property where animals respond to relative fold-changes in signals rather than absolute signal values.
The adaptive gravity model explains observed mass and velocity profiles of laboratory midge swarms.
Behavioral noise in the model allows simulated contestants to dynamically explore the effective potential landscape.
The model parameters include mobility (η = 1.0), diffusivity (D = 0.5), and various interaction parameters (α, β, δ).
The power-law exponents for self-assessment and rival assessment are typically set to values of 1 or 2.
The rate of self-inflicted fighting costs (K_self) is typically 0.01 T⁻¹, while rival-inflicted costs (K_ij) are 0.1 T⁻¹.
The model was originally developed for orb-weaving spiders (Trichonephila clavipes) and subsequently generalized.
Nonreciprocal interactions naturally arise from asymmetries in contestant strength and perception.
The framework can be extended to describe many-contestant and many-resource scenarios.
Conflict escalation is associated with effective attraction (decreasing inter-contestant distance).
Conflict de-escalation is associated with effective repulsion (increasing inter-contestant distance).
The model accounts for fighting costs that accumulate over time and can affect interaction potentials.
The paper emphasizes how modeling animal behavior motivates exploration of unique interaction types in active particle systems.
